description: Return matching rows from one dataset, filtered on ANY of its columns — state/city/county/zip shortcuts plus `where` conditions with numeric comparisons (e.g. [{field:"revenue_amt",op:"gt",value:2000000}]), sorted with `order_by` and paged with `offset`. `near` ({place:"Topeka, KS"}, a zip, or lat+lng, optional radius_miles) returns the closest rows first with distance_miles, on lists with coordinates — so "10 banks closest to Topeka" is one call for 10 rows. get_dataset lists the columns; count_locations (free) tells you how many rows match and what fetching them costs before you pay. Priced per row in USDC via x402 and settled only after the rows are produced, so a failed call costs nothing. The rate is derived from the dataset: roughly 2x its list price spread over its record count, so a small slice of a big file is cents. By default you get and pay for every matching row, up to 100 to 1,000 rows per call depending on how wide the dataset's rows are (count_locations reports maxRowsPerCall); pass limit for fewer. Call it without payment first: the result is an x402 PaymentRequired quote with the exact amount and `quote` (the same rows, each source at its rate, as count_locations' slice), and nothing is charged until you retry with payment. A paid call is billed for the rows it returns: each row at its own list's per-row rate (an Overture open-data row at $0.005; a row of a chain LocationLists sells its own list for, at that list's rate), plus a $0.01 per-call fee, rounded once to the nearest cent, at least $0.02, never more than the whole list. count_locations with the same filters, limit and offset quotes exactly that page, row source by row source (price.breakdown), before anything is paid. How a list is sold: our own lists are sold as a whole file (create_checkout / buy_dataset), and those of 5,000 records or more are also sold by the row (query_locations / create_query_checkout); smaller lists are sold whole only. Open map data lists (soldBy "row" in get_dataset) are sold by the row ONLY, at any size — there is no file to buy. One card checkout downloads up to 10,000 rows at once; up to 150,000 rows, an answer's buy link still sells them all, and the file is built after payment and its download link emailed. For more, buy the whole file where the list has one, narrow the question to a state, metro or area, or email kyle@locationlists.com for the whole file. To cover several chains near one place, pass datasets or category and a total (up to 1,000 rows) instead of dataset: one answer, one price and one file, with source_dataset naming each row's dataset and duplicates removed; inside a combined answer, small datasets are sold by the row too.

area_columns.description: Census, NOAA, FEMA and USDA facts added to EVERY ROW as columns named <kind>_<attribute>, each as "<kind>:<attribute>,<attribute>", e.g. "county:population,median_household_income" — the county / ZIP / metro / state figures beside each location, in the preview and in the file you buy, after the area's id and name (county_fips, county_name; zip_code; metro_cbsa, metro_name; state_code, state_name). Free. The same attribute words area_where takes (listed there).

area_where.description: Only rows whose county/zip/state/metro meets a Census condition, each as "<kind>:<attribute><op><value>" (ops > >= < <= =; values accept 1M, 250k, $50,000, 10%), e.g. "county:population>1000000". Every clause must hold; the fact is the area's, not the row's, and it adds nothing to the price. Attributes: e.g. population, households, median_household_income, median_age, pct_65_plus, housing_units; Census ACS people, income, education and housing; businesses and jobs by NAICS sector (<sector>_establishments, <sector>_employees) or detailed code (naics_<code>_establishments / _employees / _payroll); population growth; NOAA climate normals and actuals; NOAA storm events; station weather normals; hourly weather normals; building stock; Zillow home values; Zillow rents; building permits; IRS tax returns; FEMA hazard risk; USDA farm census. Every key (11,012) with its label, unit and kinds: GET /area-attributes.json.

areas_in.description: Only rows in these areas, e.g. {"by": "county", "ids": ["18039"]} for Elkhart County, IN — the ids count_by_area returns. Rows are placed by county_fips, county + state, coordinates or ZIP, the same as count_by_area.

ids.description: County FIPS, 5-digit ZIP, CBSA code or state code — the `id` of a count_by_area row

category.description: Instead of dataset: every dataset of one kind — "retail" (store chains), an industry or subcategory, or a kind of business such as "restaurant" or "bank branch" (search_datasets names these)

dataset.description: Dataset slug, e.g. nonprofits-va. To combine several, give datasets or category instead.

datasets.description: Instead of dataset: several dataset slugs answered as one (one count, one preview, one price, one file)

exclude.description: With category or datasets: dataset slugs left out (a category minus one of its members, e.g. a list's competitors are its own category with itself excluded)

limit.description: Rows to return and pay for. Default: every matching row, up to the most one call can return. That maximum depends on how wide the dataset's rows are, from 100 to 1,000; count_locations reports it as maxRowsPerCall, and a larger limit is reduced to it before pricing.

metro.description: Only rows in one metro area (CBSA): its 5-digit code ("37980") or its name ("Philadelphia", "Philadelphia, PA"). The same as areas_in {"by": "metro", "ids": [code]}: rows are placed the way count_by_area places them, so "all hospitals in the Philadelphia metro" is one count, one price and one purchase.

near.description: Distance search on lists with map coordinates (distanceSearch in search results): ONE of place, zip, lat+lng or `points` (within reach of ANY). Rows come back nearest first with a distance_miles column (straight line; no drive time); limit for 'the 10 closest', radius_miles for 'everything within 25 miles'. Rows without coordinates are excluded and counted.

place.description: City or town with state, e.g. "Topeka, KS" (a neighborhood or misspelling falls back to the nearest Census place name, and the answer says which).

points.description: Several points instead of one place/zip/lat+lng (at most 10): a row counts when it is within the radius of ANY of them, e.g. an operator's offices.

place.description: City or town with state, e.g. "Topeka, KS"

radius_miles.description: Only rows within this straight-line distance of the point (or of any of the points). Free.

offset.description: Skip this many matching rows, to page past the first call

order_by.description: Return the top rows by one column, e.g. {field: 'revenue_amt'} for the largest first. Blanks sort last.

permits.description: Only rows with a BUILDING PERMIT nearby, read live from the city's own permit register at question time — e.g. {"dataset": "<slug>", "city": "Austin", "state": "TX", "permits": {"days": 90, "type": "commercial", "min_usd": 1000000}}. One city register per question (from the base set's city, a ZIP in it, its county, or a state with one register); the cities read now: New York, NY; Los Angeles, CA; Chicago, IL; Dallas, TX; Austin, TX; San Francisco, CA; Seattle, WA; Nashville, TN. A kind or amount a register cannot tell is refused in words, never answered as any. Free: counts, a preview, the price of the matching rows; the openData block names the register, its publisher, licence and when it was read. On /find: &permits=1&permits_days=90&permits_type=commercial&permits_min_usd=1000000. Not sold through a checkout yet: the answer's link is the page.

days.description: Issued in the last N days (default 365)

metres.description: How close a permit must be to the row, in metres (default 60)

min_usd.description: Valuation at least this many dollars

shape.description: CRM-ready columns: hubspot (Company name, Company domain name, Website URL, Phone number, Street address, Street address 2, City, State/Region, Postal code, Country/Region, Industry, Description) or salesforce (Name, Website, Phone, BillingStreet, BillingCity, BillingState, BillingPostalCode, BillingCountry, Industry, Description) first, then every other column of the list under its own name. Nothing is dropped; a CRM column the list lacks is present and blank.

state.description: Shortcut for where state eq <value>. Two-letter code; several states comma-separated ("VA,NC,SC") are one `in`.

total.description: With datasets or category: rows to return and pay for across all of them (default every distinct match, up to 1,000), in one payment

where.description: Conditions on any column, all of which must hold. Blank cells never satisfy a comparison (the answer counts rows excluded only for that, and a small answer says what each condition removed).

any_of.description: With op any_of: the conditions, any one of which keeps the row.

field.description: Column name as listed by get_dataset (columns[].name), e.g. revenue_amt

op.description: eq/ne: case-insensitive (numeric when both sides are numbers; yes/true/y/1 are one answer). gt/gte/lt/lte: numeric, else text order (ISO dates work). in/not_in: value is an array. contains/not_contains/starts_with: text. is_blank/not_blank: no value (N/A, <UNAVAIL> count as blank). any_of: no value; kept when ANY condition in any_of holds.
